title: Lunch on Sofokleous
short: Sofokleous is the one quiet good street in the walled town. The bazaar noise stops at the corner. Nireas, at number twenty-two, has been the Tsikis family's since nineteen eighty-nine: a pergola of jasmine and bougainvillea, a vine that has been growing over the tables for twenty-five years. Symi shrimp. Grilled dorade. Panna cotta with figs, and it is your birthday, so ask for the candle. If you want the plated version instead, Romios at number fifteen revives forgotten Rhodian recipes: lamb kapamas, octopus with orange. Either way, ask if they have pitaroudia, the island's chickpea fritters. Pause the album. Eat.
long:
Sofokleous is the one quiet good street in the walled town. You can hear it happen: the bazaar noise stops at the corner. This is where lunch is, and it is your birthday, so the album stops here for a while.

Nireas, at number twenty-two, has belonged to the Tsikis family since nineteen eighty-nine. You eat under a pergola of jasmine, honeysuckle and bougainvillea, with a grapevine overhead that has been growing across the tables for twenty-five years, on a little square where the noise simply ends. The dishes people name again and again are the Symi shrimp, tiny and sweet, from the island you can see on a clear day; scallops; calamari; grilled dorade; shrimp saganaki. Then the homemade desserts, and this is where a birthday becomes a birthday: panna cotta with figs, or the chocolate mousse cake. Ask for the candle.

If you want the plated, celebratory version instead, Romios at number fifteen is fifty metres away. The chef-owner, Silouani Vlachou, was born on the island and revives forgotten Rhodian recipes: lamb kapamas, the Easter roast of the villages; cuttlefish risotto; octopus with orange. She plates them, in her own words, as art pieces, in a lantern-lit garden.

Whichever it is, order one thing for the quest. Pitaroudia. Big plump fritters of ground chickpeas with onion, grated tomato and spearmint, shallow-fried. They are the island's national dish, and they are a lunch order, not something you can buy in a shop, so this is the place. And if there is souma on the table, the island's clear grape spirit from the mountain villages, it is being distilled this very week, straight after the harvest. A shot over two ice cubes turns milky. It smells of grape, not aniseed.

A few facts to go with the food, since you have time. Rhodian cooking uses bulgur where the rest of Greece uses rice, cumin in fillings and doughs, sesame on everything, and honey to bind rather than sugar. The most Rhodian sweet of all is melekouni, a soft diamond of honey and toasted sesame with almonds and spice, which was the official treat at village weddings and was sent to relatives who could not attend, the way sugared almonds are elsewhere. It comes with a wish: may you live as many years as there are sesame seeds in the piece. You will buy one on the way up the bazaar street after lunch, and eat it later on the mole with that wish attached.

Take your time. The clock tower is open all afternoon, the mosque and the library are three minutes from the top of the bazaar, and Mandraki is not going anywhere. When you are done, walk north to Hippocrates Square and turn left up Sokratous, the bazaar street, toward the pink mosque at the top. The next track starts under the minaret.

title: Under the Minaret
short: At the top of the bazaar street: the rose-pink Suleymaniye Mosque, the first mosque of the conquest, rebuilt in eighteen oh eight, its minaret re-erected in a restoration that took seventeen years. On Christmas Day fifteen twenty-two Suleiman rode into this town through a gate on the south wall, then had the gate sealed so nobody could use his door again. It stayed shut until nineteen twenty-two. Across the lane is a library of seventeen ninety-three that holds a chronicle of the siege, written by the winners. And beside you, the clock tower: fifty-three steps, four windows, one drink included. Climb it. It is your birthday.
long:
At the top of Sokratous, the old bazaar street, the lane opens and there is a rose-pink mosque with a tall thin minaret. This is the Suleymaniye, the first mosque of the conquest, raised right after fifteen twenty-two on the site of a church whose columns you can still see in the portico. What stands here is the rebuild of eighteen oh eight. The minaret was pulled down as unsafe in nineteen eighty-seven and put back in a restoration that ran until two thousand and five. The interior has been closed since twenty fourteen and opens only irregularly. Look from outside.

This is where the story changes operating system. On the twenty-second of December fifteen twenty-two the town accepted Suleiman's terms. On Christmas Day the Sultan rode in, by tradition through the Gate of Saint Athanasios on the south wall, and came as far as the church of Saint John. Then he had that gate sealed, so that nobody could ever use his door again. It stayed shut for four hundred years, until nineteen twenty-two. On the twenty-ninth of December he came in again by the Red Gate, went down to the harbour, and admired the great chain that closed it. On the last day of the year he received the Grand Master in his tent, a man of nearly sixty who had held out for six months, and, the story says, told his vizier it was not without some compunction that he compelled this venerable warrior at his age to seek a new home. That last line is later tradition. The rest is record.

For the next three hundred and ninety years this was an Ottoman town. The Greeks were moved outside the walls into suburbs. The churches became mosques, the Jews stayed inside, wooden balconies went up over the alleys, hammams and fountains appeared, and the Knights' inns became houses and bathhouses. The city you have been walking through is not a medieval city. It is four cities stacked, and the Ottoman one is the thickest layer.

Across the lane from the mosque is the Hafiz Ahmed Agha Library, founded in seventeen ninety-three by a village boy from this island who rose to become the Sultan's chief equerry and endowed it, in his own words, for the literate public of his hometown. He even paid the librarians to teach Arabic so that people could read the books. About twelve hundred and sixty manuscripts survive inside, among them a Koran of fifteen forty and a chronicle of the siege of fifteen twenty-two, written by the winning side. The courtyard is free if the door is open; the hours are posted on the door and nowhere else, and one recent visitor found it locked because the man with the door code had gone to the hairdresser. If you play games, this is the town's arcane library, and the custodian literally holds the key.

And beside you, the Roloi, the clock tower, built in eighteen fifty-two by an Ottoman governor on a Byzantine base and rebuilt after the explosion four years later. Fifty-three steep wooden steps to a tiny chamber with four small windows. North, the Palace. West, the acropolis hill. East, the harbour and your own ship. South-east, the minaret you are standing under. The ticket is five euros and it includes a drink in the courtyard bar, beer, wine, coffee or juice, which makes it the obvious place for the birthday toast. Only about four people fit at the top. Go up. Take the drink down at the bottom afterward, and then we go back down the bazaar to buy a relic.

title: Sorcerer-Smiths
short: Walk back down the bazaar. Somewhere on this street, buy a bar of melekouni; the label must say PGI. Keep it for the mole. At the bottom, cross Hippocrates Square and go north past the museum to Symi Square, just inside the Liberty Gate. The fenced tumble of column drums there is a temple of Aphrodite, third century BC, the only ancient temple you can touch inside the walls. This is the place for the island's first inhabitants: the Telchines. Sorcerer-smiths. They forged the sickle of Cronus, summoned rain and hail, changed shape, and had the evil eye.
long:
Walk back down the bazaar street, and somewhere between the mosque and the square, in one of the small delis, buy a bar of melekouni. The label must say PGI, the protected name. A soft diamond of honey and toasted sesame. It comes with a wish, and you will eat it on the mole. If you see souma, the grape spirit, in a small bottle, that is the other quest item.

At the bottom of the street cross Hippocrates Square and go north, past Museum Square, to a small open square just inside the Liberty Gate, with a fenced tumble of column drums and blocks in it. That is a temple of Aphrodite, third century before Christ, built within a generation of the Colossus. It is the only ancient temple you can touch inside the walls, and it is the right place to go back before the Knights, before the Romans, before the statue, to the beginning.

Strabo says the island was once called Telchinis, after the Telchines who lived on it. Who were they? Diodorus says they were children of the Sea, and that they nursed the infant Poseidon. They were the first to work iron and bronze. They forged the sickle with which Cronus unmanned the sky, and, later tradition adds, the trident of Poseidon. They were the first to make statues of the gods. They could summon clouds and rain and hail at will, and even snow. They could change their shape. They were jealous of teaching their arts to anyone. Strabo's other tradition calls them maligners and sorcerers, who poured the water of the Styx mixed with sulphur on animals and crops to kill them. Ovid gives them the evil eye: eyes whose corrupting power shot forth, so that Jupiter, in disgust, thrust them under his brother's waves. Diodorus says they foresaw the flood and left.

Here is why this ruin is the place. A Telchine named Halia bore Poseidon six sons and a daughter. When Aphrodite, sailing from Cythera to Cyprus, tried to land on Rhodes, the arrogant sons drove her away, and the goddess in her wrath brought madness on them. Their mother threw herself into the sea. The daughter was Rhodos. And when the gods drew lots for the earth, Helios the sun was away driving his chariot and got no share; offered a second draw, he refused, because he had seen, growing from the bottom of the grey sea, a rich land for men. He claimed the rising island, married Rhodos, and named the island after her. Their seven sons were astrologer-kings who invented the division of the day into hours. The cleverest was murdered by his brothers out of envy, and the murderers fled to other islands, and the ones who stayed named the three cities.

So: a lost guild of artificer-warlocks, weather magic, the sickle of Cronus, a goddess's curse, a divine flood, and a sun god who won an island by declining a lottery. That is the mythic bedrock, and everything else, the Knights, the Sultan, the Italians, is built on it.

Now, thirty metres north, the Liberty Gate. The Italians cut it through the wall in nineteen twenty-four and named it for themselves, as liberators from the Ottomans. When you walk through it you leave the medieval city and the score opens up. Sea, sky, the boulevard, the harbour. Go through.

title: The City-Taker
short: You are outside the walls, on the Italian boulevard the fascists called the Foro Italico. Walk north along the harbour. On your left, the seven-sided market, closed for restoration; the Governor's Palace, built to look like the Doge's Palace in Venice; a Gothic church rebuilt from engravings of the one that exploded. All of it nineteen twenties stage-set. And as you walk, the siege of three hundred and five BC. Demetrius the Besieger built a tower nine storeys high, plated in iron, pushed by three thousand four hundred men. The Rhodians burned it, undermined it, and, one version says, drowned it in sewage. He left. They sold his machines. With the money, they built a god.
long:
You are outside the walls now, on the wide boulevard along Mandraki harbour that the Italians laid out in the nineteen twenties and called the Foro Italico. Walk north, with the water on your right. The buildings on your left are a stage set. Italy took the island from the Ottomans in nineteen twelve and kept it until nineteen forty-seven, and the governor's architect, Florestano Di Fausto, built a garden city here in a style he called Mediterranean-ness: the seven-sided market with the domed fish pavilion in its courtyard, closed this year for restoration; the Bank of Greece, once the Banca d'Italia, dressed up in Knights' masonry; the Governor's Palace, striped pink and white, a straight copy of the Doge's Palace in Venice; and the Gothic church of the Annunciation, rebuilt from old engravings of the Knights' church of Saint John that blew up in eighteen fifty-six, so that an occupying power could look as if it had always belonged here.

But walk, and let me tell you about the machine.

In three hundred and five BC, when the sea assault on the harbour behind you failed, Demetrius the Besieger turned to the land walls and built the Helepolis, the City-Taker. Diodorus gives its stats. A base almost fifty cubits square, framed of squared timber fastened with iron. Eight solid wheels, each rim two cubits wide and overlaid with heavy iron plates. Corner posts nearly a hundred cubits high, nine storeys, each floor with shuttered ports shaped to the missiles it fired: stone-throwers below, dart-throwers above. The three exposed sides were covered with iron plates nailed on so that it should receive no injury from fire carriers. And to move it, three thousand four hundred men excelling in strength. Plutarch, who gives lower numbers, marvelled that it did not totter or lean when it moved but advanced evenly, with much noise and great impetus. Vitruvius weighs it at three hundred and sixty thousand Roman pounds, about a hundred and eighteen tonnes.

How do you stop a siege construct? Three ways, all attested. One night, at about the second watch, the Rhodians hit it with an unremitting shower of fire missiles until the iron plates were dislodged and the wood beneath began to burn; Demetrius dragged it out of range, and at dawn his men counted more than eight hundred fire missiles and fifteen hundred catapult bolts on the ground. Underground, a Rhodian counter-mine met his sappers, and a citizen named Athenagoras pretended to betray the city and lured a senior officer up through the tunnel to be captured. And Vitruvius tells the third, which is the one to remember: the city's engineer Diognetus had a hole cut in the wall opposite the tower and had every citizen pour through it all the water, filth and mud that could be procured, so that when the Helepolis advanced, it sank in the quagmire. In defensive operations, Vitruvius concludes, ingenuity is of more avail than machines.

Peace came in three hundred and four. Rhodes stayed free, ungarrisoned, and kept its revenue. Demetrius sailed away and left his engines behind. The Rhodians sold them for three hundred talents, and with the money they commissioned Chares of Lindos, a pupil of Alexander's own sculptor, to build a bronze Helios seventy cubits high. It took twelve years. The wonder of the world was the scrap value of a failed siege.

You will see the deer columns ahead at the harbour mouth. That is where the statue's story ends, and where everybody has always put its feet. Go there.

title: Where Was the Colossus?
short: Two stone columns, a bronze stag and a bronze doe, sixty-two metres apart. Every postcard puts the Colossus's feet here. It never stood here. Look across the water to the fort on the mole and the windmills: in thirteen ninety-four a visiting notary was told the statue had one foot on each. That is several hundred metres. No bronze figure can stride it, and Pliny saw the wreck lying on ground you could walk around. So where? A ring of stones under the fort, says one scholar. The acropolis hill, says another. And the best current answer: the hill under the Palace, where you stood at eleven o'clock. Now walk the mole to the fort, and eat the melekouni.
long:
Two limestone columns at the harbour mouth, a bronze stag on one and a bronze doe on the other, sixty-two metres of water between them. They were put up in nineteen thirty-nine by the Italian administration, and every postcard and every guide will tell you that the Colossus of Rhodes stood astride this entrance with ships passing between its legs. Stand here and read the dedication that was carved on its pedestal, because that at least is real: To thy very self, O Sun, did the people of Dorian Rhodes raise high to heaven this colossus, when, having laid to rest the brazen wave of war, they crowned their country with the spoils of their foes. Not only over the sea, but on the land too, did they establish the lovely light of unfettered freedom.

Now the facts. Chares of Lindos finished it around two hundred and eighty BC: thirty-three metres of bronze plate over an iron frame, braced inside with stone, a nude youth with long curling hair and a crown of rays, the Helios of the Rhodian coins. No torch; the torch was invented by a Dutch engraver in fifteen seventy-two. It stood about sixty-six years. Then an earthquake broke it at the knees. The King of Egypt offered three thousand talents and a hundred master builders to raise it again, and an oracle told the Rhodians not to, and they left the god lying. It lay there for centuries. Pliny the Elder saw it: even lying on the ground it is a marvel. Few people can make their arms meet round the thumb, and the fingers are larger than most statues; where the limbs have broken off, enormous cavities yawn, and inside are seen great masses of rock with the weight of which the artist steadied it. Nobody in antiquity wrote down where it lay.

The harbour-straddling picture is medieval. Its earliest trace is a notary from Campania named Niccolò de Martoni, who came through in thirteen ninety-four and wrote down what the locals told him: one foot on the end of the mole where the church of Saint Nicholas stood, and the other on the mole where the mills are. Look across the water. The fort at the end of the mole is on the church's site, and the windmills are on the other mole. That is several hundred metres. A thirty-three metre figure cannot stride it. Engineers add that bronze legs splayed even twelve metres would buckle under the weight, and that a statue which fell across the harbour mouth would have closed the port, whereas Pliny walked around it on land. The picture was fixed forever in fifteen seventy-two, when Philips Galle engraved Maarten van Heemskerck's design of the sun god bestriding the harbour with a smoking torch, and it descended from there into Shakespeare, he doth bestride the narrow world like a colossus, and into Emma Lazarus's poem on the Statue of Liberty, not like the brazen giant of Greek fame, with conquering limbs astride from land to land.

And the ending everyone loves: in the year six hundred and fifty-four, the Arabs overran Rhodes, sold the bronze to a Jewish merchant of Edessa, and he carried it away on nine hundred camels. One source says nine hundred and eighty. Every version traces to a single lost chronicle, the arithmetic does not work, a pagan bronze scrapheap is unlikely to have survived the Christian centuries, and the newest study calls it a fabrication modelled on the shattered statue in the Book of Daniel. Nine hundred camels remains the best line in the story. Keep it as a story.

So where did it stand? Three answers. Under the floor of the fort at the end of the mole there is a ring of sandstone blocks nobody can explain, and finely cut curved marble reused in its walls; a German scholar argued in two thousand and three that the pedestal was there. On the acropolis hill to the west, the one with the four columns, another scholar re-identified the temple as the sanctuary of Helios and the ruin beside it as the statue's base and workshop. And in twenty twenty-four, in what reviewers call the definitive study, Nathan Badoud put the sanctuary of Helios on the small hill at the head of the Knights' quarter, where an inscription naming the sacred area of Helios, dedications by his priests, and the marble head you saw this morning were all found. The hill under the Palace. Where you stood at eleven o'clock, in the courtyard, looking north-east toward the Turkish coast.

Now walk out along the mole to the fort, past the windmills, and turn around. From there you can see the whole impossible stride, and the hill, and the ship you came on. Eat the melekouni. May you live as many years as there are sesame seeds in the piece.

title: Fort Saint Nicholas
short: You are at the end of the mole. The round fort was built in the fourteen sixties on the site of a chapel of Saint Nicholas, ringed with a bastion after fourteen eighty, a lighthouse on top since the sixteen hundreds. It was the first thing the Ottomans attacked in fourteen eighty: weeks of bombardment from the shore by the cemetery you can see across the water, then assaults across a pontoon bridge, until an English sailor swam out one night and cut the bridge's anchor. Turn around. Walls, windmills, the Italian boulevard, the Palace hill, Turkey on the horizon, your ship. The interior is closed. The view is free.
long:
You are at the end of the mole, and this is Fort Saint Nicholas: a round tower built between fourteen sixty-four and fourteen sixty-seven by Grand Master Zacosta on the site of a chapel of Saint Nicholas, patron of sailors, that was already here in thirteen ninety-four. After the first siege d'Aubusson wrapped it in the low bastion you can see. A lighthouse has burned on the roof since the sixteen hundreds and still does. The interior has been under restoration for years and you should treat it as closed. The mole is public, and the view from here is the best free thing in the town.

This tower is where the siege of fourteen eighty began. The Ottoman commander was Mesih Pasha, and he is worth a moment: born into the last Byzantine imperial family, probably a nephew of the last emperor of Constantinople, taken at the age of ten when the city fell in fourteen fifty-three, converted, raised as a palace page, and sent back twenty-seven years later to besiege Christians for the Sultan. He arrived on the twenty-third of May with about a hundred and sixty ships and seventy thousand men, against perhaps five hundred knights and two thousand soldiers. His first target was this tower, because it controlled both harbours. His big bombards fired at it across the water from the ground around the Ottoman cemetery you can see on the far shore, beside the casino. On the ninth of June the Janissaries stormed it and were thrown back. Then, on the night of the eighteenth of June, they pushed a floating bridge toward the mole for a night assault. According to the Order's own chronicle, an English sailor named Roger Jervis swam out in the dark, found the anchor by which the bridge was to be warped into place, cut the rope and carried the anchor off, so that the bridge drifted useless. The assault that followed cost the Ottomans two or three thousand men. A German engineer who had deserted to the Knights and offered them his marvellous genius turned out to be a spy, and was hanged in the public square.

The Ottomans then moved their guns to the weak south-east corner of the walls, by the Jewish quarter, and pounded it to rubble, and on the twenty-seventh of July twenty-five hundred Janissaries got over the wall. You heard about that from the ramparts. D'Aubusson took a lance through the breastplate. The attack broke. On the seventeenth of August the fleet sailed away, and Mehmed the Conqueror, who had taken Constantinople, died the following year without ever taking Rhodes. Forty-two years later his great-grandson came back.

Now turn around and look. From left to right: the windmills on the mole, three survivors of thirteen that ground grain for the Knights' galleys. The great wall with the twin towers of the Marine Gate. The Palace on its hill, where the sun god's sanctuary probably was. The pink-and-white Governor's Palace and the Italian boulevard. The deer columns and the harbour mouth. And out to the east, on a clear day, the mountains of Turkey, the Peraia, which Rhodes ruled when the statue was new. Badoud's argument is that the Colossus was placed to be seen from there: a bronze sun over the water, telling the mainland who held dominion, in the epigram's words, both on land and sea.

Behind you is the open sea, and the direction your ship will take tonight. Walk back along the mole. The birthday cocktail is waiting on the quay.

title: Birthday
short: This track has no history in it. Walk back along the mole to the quay by the closed market, where three floating decks are moored: Swan by Kontiki. Go to the top deck. Order something unnecessary. Face the harbour mouth. You have walked four thousand years today, and it is your birthday. [Insert the birthday message or the song here.]
long:
This track has no history in it.

Walk back along the mole, past the windmills, to the inner quay by the closed market, where three floating decks are moored off the square. That is Swan by Kontiki. Go up to the top deck. Order something unnecessary. Face the harbour mouth, so that the fort, the windmills and the walls are all in front of you and the sun is over your shoulder.

You have walked four thousand years today, from a sorcerers' island to a Fascist boulevard, through a hospital, a guild street, an exploded church, a dictator's unused palace, a dragon gate, a mile of ramparts, a synagogue, a bazaar, a mosque and a library, past the impossible feet of a bronze god. And it is your birthday.

[This is where the personal track goes. A song that matters. A message recorded by someone who could not be here, spliced in as a ghost voice. Or thirty seconds of nothing but the harbour.]

When the glass is empty, the last track is the walk back to the ship, along the water, past a broken tower. Take your time. All-aboard is five-thirty, and it is a level fifteen-minute walk.

title: Return by Sea
short: Walk south along the quay, out through the gardens by Saint Paul's Gate, to the mole beyond it. The stump of stone at its root is the Tower of Naillac: forty-six metres high once, a lighthouse-keep that held one end of the great harbour chain, split by the earthquake of eighteen sixty-three and pulled down. The last of the fortifications to die, and not to an army. Then along the water to the ship. Helios. Rome. Byzantium. The Knights. Suleiman. The Juderia. Italy. Greece. You. Rhodes has spent its history watching ships arrive. This time you are the one leaving.
long:
Walk south along the quay, with the water on your left, past the gardens outside the walls and the round bastion of Saint Paul's Gate, to the mole that runs out beyond it. The broken stump of masonry at the root of that mole is the last set-piece of the day.

This was the Tower of Naillac, built between thirteen ninety-six and fourteen twenty-one by the Grand Master of that name: a square keep forty-six metres high, lighthouse and watchtower, and the anchor of the great chain that closed the commercial harbour every night, the chain Suleiman came down to admire in December fifteen twenty-two. It survived both sieges. It survived the explosion of eighteen fifty-six. Then, at half past nine in the evening on the twenty-second of April eighteen sixty-three, an earthquake of about magnitude seven and a half threw down two thousand houses on the island and split the tower, and the Ottoman administration pulled the rest of it down. The last of the fortifications of Rhodes to die, killed not by an army but by the ground itself.

From here it is a level walk of about twelve minutes along the waterfront to the ship. Let me compress the day as you go.

Helios, the sun, who missed the lottery of the gods and claimed this island as it rose from the sea. The Telchines, who forged the sickle of Cronus and were drowned for their arrogance. Phorbas, who killed the snakes. Tlepolemus, who took nine ships to Troy. Demetrius, whose iron tower sank in the mud, and whose scrap paid for a bronze god thirty-three metres tall that stood for sixty-six years and lay in pieces for eight hundred. The Romans, who came here to learn to speak: Cicero, and a young Julius Caesar, who was kidnapped by pirates on the way and read them his poems for thirty-eight days. The Byzantines, who built the first citadel on the sun god's hill. The Knights, who came in thirteen ten, ran the island as a guild of eight nations, built a hospital before they built a palace, killed a dragon that was probably a crocodile, held Mehmed's army in fourteen eighty and lost to Suleiman's in fifteen twenty-two, and sailed out of this harbour with drums beating. The Ottomans, who moved the Greeks outside the walls and kept the city for four centuries. The Jews of the Juderia, who spoke the Spanish of their grandparents here until July nineteen forty-four. The Italians, who rebuilt the Palace for a king who never came, and cut a gate in the wall and named it Liberty. The Greeks, who took the island back on the seventh of March nineteen forty-eight and named a square for the day. And the tourists, and the cruise ships, and you.

Rhodes is not remarkable because it preserves one moment. It is remarkable because nobody ever stopped using it. Every conqueror kept the same walls, the same streets, the same hill, and added a layer. You walked down through all of them this morning and back up this afternoon, and the city did not mind.

The ship is getting larger ahead of you. Rhodes has spent three thousand years watching ships arrive. This time, you are the one leaving. Sunset is at six fifty-four, from the top deck, with this wall sliding astern. Happy birthday.

title: B-side: The Killing Ground
short: An optional track, for the moat. Enter by the gardens at Saint Paul's Gate, or beside the port at the Akandia Gate, and walk the dry ditch clockwise. Never filled with water. About thirty metres wide, under walls up to twelve metres thick, now a park with cannonballs in the grass. You have heard about the walls from inside and from on top. This is what an attacking army had to cross. Under the d'Amboise Gate, past the pentagonal Saint George bastion, the Tower of Spain, the English curtain, to the great round drum at the harbour corner where the first siege broke through. An hour to ninety minutes. Free, always open.
long:
This is an optional track, a B-side, for the moat. If the day runs long, skip it. If the ship lands you at Akandia, this is the best way to start the morning, from the gate beside the port, and it comes out at Mandraki.

The Knights' moat was never filled with water. It is a dry ditch, roughly thirty metres wide, cut along the whole landward side of the town under walls up to twelve metres thick, with a second, outer wall on the far side and a sloping glacis beyond that. It is now a landscaped park with sandy paths, lawns, an open-air theatre, and stone cannonballs lying where they fell in fourteen eighty and fifteen twenty-two. It is free and open at all hours, lit after dark, with no kiosks inside. Enter by the gardens at Saint Paul's Gate at the Mandraki end, or beside the port at the Akandia Gate, or by the stairways down from the gates of Saint Anthony and Saint Athanasios. Walking the whole thing takes an hour to ninety minutes.

You have heard about these walls from inside, and you may have walked on top of them. This is the third view: the one an attacking army had.

Going clockwise from Mandraki, you pass under the twin round towers of the d'Amboise Gate, with the drawbridge slots above you, and then the pentagonal Bastion of Saint George: stand in the ditch and look up at the sloped face and the low cannon ports at moat level, designed to rake this exact ground at short range. Behind it the terreplein of Spain, an earth-and-stone bank built after fourteen eighty to absorb cannon fire, was honeycombed with galleries designed to be collapsed on any attacker who got inside.

Then the Tower of Spain, where the Janissaries planted their banners at noon on the twenty-fourth of September fifteen twenty-two and were driven off through the tunnels. Then the long English curtain, where forty Ottoman mines came under this ditch and Tadini's drum listened for them. Then the gate of Saint John, the Red Gate. And at the harbour corner, the great round drum of the del Carretto bastion, built by Grand Master Fabrizio del Carretto exactly on the spot where, at dawn on the twenty-seventh of July fourteen eighty, twenty-five hundred Janissaries took the Tower of Italy and planted their standards, and d'Aubusson climbed his brick retrenchment three times and took five wounds, and the Order's vice-chancellor, Caoursin, reported that the Turks saw above the wall a splendid golden cross and a virgin all in white carrying a shield and spear, and broke. How else, Caoursin asked, could so small an army overcome such a powerful enemy? It was printed within months and became a European bestseller. Propaganda, brilliantly done. Walk inside the bastion if it is open, and feel how thick the cannon platform is. The bastion is the scar tissue.

The Akandia Gate beside it was cut by the Italians in nineteen thirty-five and brings you out beside the port, five minutes from the ship.

title: B-side: Kallithea Springs
short: An optional track, for a taxi. Fifteen minutes south of the port, on a cove of red rock, the Italians built a spa in nineteen twenty-nine: Art Deco with Moorish arches, a small rotunda with six gates and a statue of Eros over the spring, a great rotunda with a curved arcade above the sea, every path a black-and-white pebble mosaic. The Germans made it a prison camp. It was a ruin by nineteen sixty-seven, and The Guns of Navarone was filmed in the ruin. Restored in two thousand and seven. The spring has dried. Swim off the rocks. Five euros. Open until eight.
long:
An optional track, for a taxi, and for the birthday. Ask at the rank by the port for Kallithea Springs, Thermes Kallitheas: about fifteen minutes and fifteen to twenty euros south along the east coast. Agree the fare first. Open until eight, five euros to enter, and bring swim shoes, because the entry to the water is rock.

For centuries, reddish water surged out of a rock formation in this cove, and the locals of the Ottoman era called it Tsilonero and swore by it for arthritis, skin and asthma. In nineteen twenty-seven the Italian governor commissioned a scientific study, and in nineteen twenty-eight he handed the site to an architect named Pietro Lombardi, with Armando Bernabiti on decoration. What they built was inaugurated on the first of July nineteen twenty-nine: Art Deco with Moorish teeth. A small rotunda, fourteen metres across, with six gates in the Moorish style around a statue of Eros, built directly over the spring, with six fountains feeding a central pool. A larger rotunda whose curved arcade of benches looks over the bay, its dome carried on two half-domes. Every path paved in black-and-white pebble mosaics of plants and geometry. The outer walls painted with sea creatures. In the nineteen thirties it hosted an international congress of hydrologists and a jet-set clientele.

Then the war. The Germans turned the complex into a penitentiary; barbed wire and minefields had transformed the once impressive spa into a place of dismay, says the site's own history. It reopened in fits on Marshall Aid money and closed for good in nineteen sixty-seven. Hollywood found the ruin first. The Guns of Navarone, nineteen sixty-one, with Peck, Niven and Quinn, was shot here; so was Escape to Athena in nineteen seventy-nine. The municipality restored it between nineteen ninety-nine and two thousand and seven and reopened it with Anthony Quinn's family present. The spring itself has dried. This is a swimming cove now, with pergolas, a cafe-bar at the water, and sunbeds.

If you play games, you already have it: an abandoned temple of a healing god at the water's edge, mosaic wards underfoot, a dry sacred spring under a rotunda shrine to Eros, and a wartime prison layer for the haunted second act.

Swim. Have the drink. Give yourself an hour and a half, and be in the taxi by a quarter to five.

title: B-side: The Hill of the Sun
short: An optional track, for the acropolis. Thirty-five minutes uphill from the Gate of Saint Athanasios, or a ten-minute taxi. Four re-erected Doric columns on the ridge they call Monte Smith, after the British admiral who watched here for Napoleon's fleet. Below them a stadium two hundred and ten metres long, an odeon, and four cave sanctuaries cut into the rock. One scholar says this temple was the sanctuary of Helios and the Colossus stood beside it; another puts the statue on the summit, as a beacon for all five harbours. From the ridge you see the whole town, both harbours, and Turkey. Sunset is the famous slot. You will be at sea for it.
long:
An optional track, for the acropolis of ancient Rhodes. Thirty-five minutes uphill from the Gate of Saint Athanasios at the south-west corner of the walls, or a ten-minute taxi from the rank by the port. Free, open-air, always open. It only fits the day if you give up the Palace interior or Mandraki, so it is here for the version of you that comes back.

The hill is called Monte Smith, after Admiral Sir Sidney Smith, the man who stopped Napoleon at Acre, who by local tradition set up an observation post here in eighteen oh two to watch for the French fleet. Every empire since the founding has posted lookouts on this ridge, because from here you can see the whole town, both harbours, the west coast, and the mountains of Turkey.

On the summit, four Doric columns and a scrap of architrave re-erected by the Italians, labelled since their excavations as the Temple of Pythian Apollo; in twenty twenty-five visitors found them fenced and scaffolded, so treat them as a silhouette. Below, the Hellenistic stadium, two hundred and ten metres long, with its curved end, its officials' seats, and the athletes' starting mechanism still in place; joggers use the track. Beside it a little marble odeon for eight hundred, almost all reconstruction. And cut into the ridge between the temples, four nymphaea: cave sanctuaries with cisterns and niches, shrines to the water nymphs, the closest thing on the hill to a real dungeon.

Here is why the Colossus question comes up here. Ursula Vedder, a German archaeologist, argued in twenty fifteen that a votive statue of Helios belongs in Helios's own precinct, re-identified this big temple as the long-lost sanctuary of the sun, and read the ruin just north-east of it as the base and the workshop where the statue was cast, in large sections in pits nearby, rather than in the rising mound of earth the ancient account describes. Robert Kebric accepted her identification but pushed the statue higher, to the limestone shelf at the very top of the hill, beside the temple of Athena and Zeus where the city kept its treaties, so that it could act as a beacon for all five harbours. His point about this hill is that only from here can you watch the sun's whole arc across the sea from rising to setting, which is why a city that worshipped the sun would put its sacred heart up here. Nathan Badoud, in twenty twenty-four, disagreed and put the sanctuary on the small hill under the Palace. Nobody has excavated to test any of it.

Walk the stadium for scale: the statue was about a sixth of its length, lying down. Stand at the temple's north-east corner and look down over the stadium and the odeon to the harbours. That is the sightline Vedder argues the statue commanded.

And two Romans, to finish. Around seventy-five BC a young Julius Caesar sailed for Rhodes to study rhetoric with Apollonius Molon, was captured by pirates on the way, laughed at them for asking only twenty talents and offered fifty, read them his poems for thirty-eight days and called them illiterate barbarians to their faces, and after his ransom came back, caught them at anchor, and crucified them, having their throats cut first as a kindness. Cicero had studied here two years earlier and came home, he said, almost transformed. And in six BC the emperor's heir Tiberius walked away from Rome and spent eight years on this island in a modest house, going to the gymnasium without his lictors and arguing with the professors. He kept an astrologer named Thrasyllus. One day, on a cliff walk, convinced the man was a fraud, he resolved to push him off, and at that moment Thrasyllus pointed at a ship in the distance and said it carried good news. It was the recall to Rome. Sunset from this ridge is the famous slot. You will be at sea for it, which is its own kind of answer.
